_about: Global sea level, metres against today's, by astronomers' year, for the Sea level curve of the Time Machine bench (experiments/time-machine.html). The same readings as stories/sea-level.json (which the map's own sea-level painting reads, by years ago), converted to the store's year (years ago subtracted from 2026) so a timeline can draw it along its span. Between points, interpolate linearly. HOW SURE: approximate. The points are read from the global ice-volume-equivalent curve of Lambeck and others (2014) and rounded to a few metres; the paper's own uncertainty is a few metres for most of the last twelve thousand years and larger before. It is one global figure: where the ice left, the land itself rose, most in Scandinavia and around Hudson Bay, and the local shore there followed the land, not this curve. Nothing a child does on the line makes the difference show, but no story should lean on a single number from here without checking the paper's table.
source: Lambeck, Rouby, Purcell, Sun and Sambridge, “Sea level and global ice volumes from the Last Glacial Maximum to the Holocene”, PNAS 111 (43): 15296–15303 (2014), doi:10.1073/pnas.1411762111; the global curve, read from the figure and rounded.
licence: The paper is © the authors and the National Academy of Sciences and is open to read; the numbers here are our approximate readings of its published curve, cited, not the paper's own table.
